title: How Does Muon Work in Private Deep Learning? Scalable Differentially Private Training via Orthogonalization

paper.title: How Does Muon Work in Private Deep Learning? Scalable Differentially Private Training via Orthogonalization
paper.abstract:
Abstract Training deep neural networks requires optimizers that balance computational efficiency with formal data privacy.
While orthogonalized update rules, such as the recently introduced Muon optimizer, have shown strong empirical performance and scalability, their behavior under Differential Privacy (DP) is not yet understood.
In this paper, we propose DP-Muon, a differentially private variant of the Muon optimizer.
By analyzing Muon’s orthogonalized updates through the lens of a Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO), we show that the leading effect of per-example clipping is a positive rescaling of the gradient, to which the LMO is blind, so that only a small directional residual controlled by the centered gradient variance enters the optimization error.
This yields an 𝒪 ( K − 1 / 4 ) \mathcal{O}(K^{-1/4}) convergence rate, up to logarithmic factors, to a clipping-dependent neighborhood at a fixed noise scale and, with noise calibrated to a fixed ( ε , δ ) (\varepsilon,\delta) budget, the standard ( d / ( n ​ ε ) ) 1 / 2 (\sqrt{d}/(n\varepsilon))^{1/2} privacy–utility bound of DP-SGD, without assuming bounded gradients. Furthermore, we investigate the hyperparameter landscape of DP-Muon and document how the optimal learning rate, momentum, and batch size change under privacy.
Empirically, on image classification DP-Muon matches or improves on DP-SGD and DP-Adam, whereas on language modeling the best optimizer depends on the batch size, with DP-Muon best at small batches and DP-Adam best near the privacy-optimal batch size.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Adaptive methods such as Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) and AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) remain the default choice for training large models ( Achiam et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . A prominent recent alternative is Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , which applies an approximate orthogonalization to the momentum of matrix-valued parameters. Muon has attracted considerable attention due to its strong empirical performance, efficient GPU implementation, and reduced optimizer-state memory; its scalability has been demonstrated by training the Moonlight 16B Mixture-of-Experts model on 5.7 trillion tokens ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Its update can be interpreted through stochastic spectral descent ( Carlson et al., 2015 ; Kovalev et al., 2018 ) and, more generally, as a step along a linear minimization oracle (LMO) over a norm ball ( Jaggi, 2013 ; Pethick et al., 2025 ) . The LMO view gives a unified treatment of non-Euclidean methods with momentum, recovering normalized SGD ( Levy, 2016 ; Cutkosky and Mehta, 2020 ) , SignSGD and Signum ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ; Sun et al., 2023 ) , Scion ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) , and Muon as special cases. In this work, we study whether, and how, the advantages of momentum orthogonalization carry over to differential privacy (DP). We consider the standard central, example-level setting of DP-SGD ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) : each per-example gradient is clipped to norm c c , Gaussian noise is added to the average, and the result is passed to the optimizer; the momentum and LMO steps are post-processing and do not affect privacy ( Dwork et al., 2014 ) . The optimization problem, however, becomes substantially more delicate. Active clipping introduces a state-dependent bias, privacy noise is injected at every step, momentum aggregates gradients along a changing trajectory, and the noisy momentum is then passed through a nonlinear map. Existing analyses of private nonconvex optimization typically sidestep active clipping: the sharpest rates assume Lipschitz losses, that is, uniformly bounded per-example gradients, so that clipping at a threshold above the bound is inactive ( Bassily et al., 2021 ; Tran and Cutkosky, 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Arora et al., 2023 ; Lowy et al., 2024 ) , and analyses of private distributed methods make similar assumptions (Appendix F ). Generic analyses of biased stochastic gradients ( Ajalloeian and Stich, 2020 ; Demidovich et al., 2023 ) measure the full additive bias and do not exploit the structure of the update.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: Our answer to the question in the title has a theoretical and an empirical part. • Clipping as rescaling. We prove the positive-ray decomposition ( 1 ) and a matching bound on the variance of clipped gradients relative to λ ⁡ ( g ) \lambda(g) (Section 3 ). • Convergence of private momentum-LMO methods. For smooth nonconvex objectives in any finite-dimensional norm (covering Muon, Scion, sign descent, and normalized SGD), we prove a high-probability bound that separates optimization error, momentum tracking, sampling noise, privacy noise, and a clipping floor ρ 1 ​ min ⁡ { σ , σ 2 / c } \rho_{1}\min\{\sigma,\sigma^{2}/c\} (Theorem 1 ). The floor is the dual-norm version of the tight Euclidean floor of clipped SGD ( Koloskova et al., 2023 ) and vanishes as σ → 0 \sigma\to 0 ; passing through the LMO thus costs at most the norm-conversion constant ρ 1 \rho_{1} relative to clipped SGD, and the guarantee does not show that it improves on it. At a fixed noise scale, the bound gives the rate 𝒪 ~ ( K − 1 / 4 ) \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(K^{-1/4}) , where 𝒪 ~ \widetilde{\mathcal{O}} hides factors logarithmic in K K and in the failure probability; and with noise calibrated to an ( ε , δ ) (\varepsilon,\delta) budget it gives the familiar 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( c ​ 𝔼 ​ ‖ Z ‖ ⋆ ​ log ⁡ ( 1 / δ ) / ( n ​ ε ) ) 1 / 2 ) \mathcal{O}\big((c\,\mathbb{E}\|Z\|_{\star}\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}/(n\varepsilon))^{1/2}\big) dependence (Corollary 1 , Appendix C.2 ). • What changes under DP. On CNN and a 30M-parameter GPT model, we sweep the batch size, learning rate, and momentum for DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon (and Scion). Under DP, the optimal batch size grows by one to two orders of magnitude and the ranking of optimizers depends on the batch size , unlike in non-private training, where Muon is best at every batch size. On CIFAR-10, DP-Muon attains the lowest mean test loss at all but one batch size, with the gaps within one standard deviation at intermediate batch sizes; on language modeling, DP-Muon is best at small batch sizes, DP-Adam near the optimal batch size, and Scion at large batch sizes (Section 4 ).

sections.heading: Concurrent work.
sections.text: Two concurrent and independent works also study private Muon 1 1 1 Both also use the name “DP-Muon” for closely related algorithms. . Kim and Fan (2026) analyze a Muon variant with finite-step Newton–Schulz (NS) orthogonalization and propose a bias-corrected DP-MuonBC; their vanishing-rate corollaries assume moment bounds on the raw (uncentered) per-example gradients and let the clipping threshold grow with the horizon, while their general bound contains a clipping term that persists even without sampling noise. Shanmugam et al. (2026) study when orthogonalization recovers useful singular directions of privatized gradients through a Wedin-type signal-to-noise argument and report large gains of DP-Muon over DP-SGD in vision at large batch sizes. Our analysis is complementary: it covers general LMO geometries, requires only centered variance, and isolates the part of the clipping bias that an LMO actually sees; a detailed comparison is given in Section 3.3 and Appendix E .

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We compare DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon (along with DP-Scion for language modeling) against their non-private counterparts on CIFAR-10 image classification ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) and on language modeling using a 30M-parameter NanoGPT model. To approximate the orthogonalization update, we utilize the Newton-Schulz method Jordan et al. (2024) with 5 iterations. DP training uses Opacus ( Yousefpour et al., 2021 ) with Poisson subsampling (our analysis uses fixed-size batches), clipping threshold c = 1 c=1 following De et al. (2022) , ε = 8 \varepsilon=8 , and δ = 1 / ( 2 ​ n ) \delta=1/(2n) . For each optimizer and batch size B B we grid-search the learning rate and the momentum 1 − α 1-\alpha , with zero weight decay; grids are listed in Appendix G . To make models compatible with per-example clipping, BatchNorm layers are replaced by GroupNorm and biases are disabled in all linear layers. We report the best value over the grid for each B B . The CIFAR-10 curves average three seeds; all language-modeling results and all heatmaps are single runs. For DP-SGD on CIFAR-10 ( B ≥ 256 B\geq 256 ) and for Scion at B = 16,384 B=16{,}384 , the best learning rate lies at the upper end of the grid (Appendix G ), so these baselines may be slightly under-tuned. Note that the hyperparameter search itself is not included in the privacy accounting, as is common in the DP literature ( Papernot and Steinke, 2022 ) . Note that we utilize standard momentum for SGD and Muon optimizers (equivalent to nesterov=False in PyTorch). Figure 1 : Best test loss as a function of batch size for SGD, Adam, and Muon. All plotted values represent the optimal configuration found across the learning rate and momentum grid search. (Left) Standard non-private training. (Right) Differentially private (DP) training for 80 epochs. We perform three independent runs to compute the reported deviation intervals.

sections.heading: Image classification.
sections.text: We train the CIFAR Airbench architecture ( Jordan, 2024 ) (2M parameters). Without privacy (Figure 1 , left), Muon attains the lowest test loss at every batch size, with its minimum (below 1.05 1.05 ) at B = 256 B=256 , whereas Adam and SGD are best at B ≤ 128 B\leq 128 . With privacy (right), the picture changes in two ways. First, all optimizers prefer batches that are one to two orders of magnitude larger, with minima at B = 5000 B=5000 – 10000 10000 , in line with prior observations for DP-SGD ( De et al., 2022 ; Sander et al., 2023 ) . Second, the gaps between optimizers largely disappear: for 128 ≤ B ≤ 1024 128\leq B\leq 1024 the three curves overlap within one standard deviation. DP-Muon attains the lowest mean loss at every batch size except B = 10000 B=10000 , where DP-SGD is marginally better, but the differences exceed one standard deviation only at the extremes B = 64 B=64 and B = 25000 B=25000 , where DP-Muon degrades the least. Across privacy levels at B = 1024 B=1024 (Appendix G.2 ), DP-Muon is on par with or slightly better than DP-SGD and DP-Adam for ε ∈ { 1 , 5 , 8 } \varepsilon\in\{1,5,8\} , with the largest margin over DP-Adam at ε = 1 \varepsilon=1 ; at ε = 3 \varepsilon=3 the three methods are within noise. Figure 2 : Language modeling (30M GPT): best loss versus batch size at the best learning rate and momentum for each batch size. Left: non-private. Right: DP ( ε = 8 \varepsilon=8 ), including Scion. Note the different batch-size and loss ranges.

sections.heading: Language modeling.
sections.text: The model consists of 6 layers, 6 attention heads, an embedding dimension of 384, and a vocabulary of 50,304 tokens. It is trained on sequences of length 1,024 for 600 million tokens from the 10-billion-token subset of FineWeb ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) , equating to roughly 20 tokens per parameter. The training set is a fixed random subset of n ≈ 5.86 ⋅ 10 5 n\approx 5.86\cdot 10^{5} sequences from this pool, processed for one epoch with Poisson sampling rate q = B / n q=B/n and δ = 1 / ( 2 ​ n ) \delta=1/(2n) ; this translates to approximately 18,300 steps for a batch size of B = 32 B=32 , down to 36 steps for a maximum batch size of B = 16,384 B=16{,}384 . We define a single sequence of 1,024 tokens as the privacy unit, so a document that spans several sequences is not protected as a whole. In the non-private baseline, the performance ranking (Muon < < Adam < < SGD) holds across all batch sizes, and Muon’s advantage grows with B B (achieving a final loss of 4.10 versus 4.82 for Adam at B = 1024 B=1024 ). Under differential privacy (right), the optimal batch size shifts from 32–64 up to 1024–4096, and the optimizer ranking becomes dependent on B B . DP-Muon has the lowest loss for B ≤ 256 B\leq 256 , by at most 0.09 0.09 nats in single runs; DP-Adam is optimal for 512 ≤ B ≤ 2048 512\leq B\leq 2048 and attains the lowest overall loss (6.33 at B = 1024 B=1024 , versus 6.51 for DP-Muon at B = 2048 B=2048 ); and DP-Scion, which utilizes sign updates for the embedding and output layers, performs best for B ≥ 4096 B\geq 4096 and exhibits the least degradation at very large batch sizes. At their respective optimal batch sizes, the four optimizers are within 0.25 nats of each other, compared to a gap of 0.9 nats between Muon and SGD without privacy.

sections.heading: What changes under privacy.
sections.text: We highlight three findings. (i) Batch size is the dominant hyperparameter on both tasks: at a fixed budget of epochs or tokens, the optimal batch size grows by a factor of 15–300, and the ranking of optimizers depends on it, so conclusions drawn at a single batch size, or transferred from non-private training, can be misleading. In both tasks the root-mean-square size of the privacy noise exceeds the root-mean-square bound c / B c/\sqrt{B} on the sampling noise of clipped gradients by one to two orders of magnitude at every batch size and decays with B B faster than B − 1 / 2 B^{-1/2} , and the observed optima lie where its norm becomes comparable to the clipping radius (Figure 3 , Appendix D.1 ). There, the noise-to-signal ratio is about 4 4 – 27 27 times larger than the admissibility condition of Theorem 1 allows for 1 − α = 0.9 1-\alpha=0.9 , so the theorem does not cover these configurations and does not explain the location of the optima (Appendix D.2 ). The dependence of the ranking on the batch size is consistent with reports of large gains for private Muon at large batches in vision ( Shanmugam et al., 2026 ) . (ii) The learning rate of DP-Muon grows with the batch size : for language modeling, from 0.05 0.05 at B ≤ 512 B\leq 512 to 0.2 0.2 at B ≥ 8192 B\geq 8192 , whereas the optimal learning rate of DP-Adam stays within [ 10 − 3 , 3 ⋅ 10 − 3 ] [10^{-3},3\cdot 10^{-3}] and, without privacy, the optimal learning rate of every method on language modeling is the same at all batch sizes (Appendix G.3 ). (iii) DP-Muon is insensitive to the momentum : for DP language modeling, at the optimal learning rate, its loss varies by about 0.1 0.1 nats or less over momentum values 1 − α ∈ [ 0.8 , 0.95 ] 1-\alpha\in[0.8,0.95] at every batch size, so the selected momentum appears erratic across batch sizes (Appendix G.3 ). This is compatible with Theorem 1 , in which a longer momentum window 1 / α 1/\alpha reduces the filtered sampling and privacy noise ( ∝ α \propto\sqrt{\alpha} ) but increases the tracking error ( ∝ L ​ γ / α \propto L\gamma/\alpha ).

sections.heading: LMO-based methods.
sections.text: Beyond Scion and the trust-region analyses of Kovalev (2025) ; Kovalev and Borodich (2025) , LMO-based methods include the layer-wise Gluon ( Riabinin et al., 2025 ) , and the effect of replacing the polar factor by a few Newton–Schulz steps is analyzed by Shulgin et al. (2025) and Kim and Oh (2026) . None of these works consider per-example clipping or privacy noise; distributed and compressed variants are discussed in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Clipping in private optimization.
sections.text: Analyses of per-example clipping are compared in Section 3.3 . A complementary line replaces clipping by per-sample normalization, which removes the threshold ( Bu et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2022 ) ; we instead keep the standard clipping of DP-SGD and normalize only the aggregated momentum through the LMO. Nonlinear post-processing of privatized gradients creates its own bias, which can be corrected for Adam ( Tang et al., 2024 ) and for Newton–Schulz ( Kim and Fan, 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Training dynamics and hyperparameters under privacy.
sections.text: Large batches are crucial for accurate private training ( De et al., 2022 ) ; Sander et al. (2023) show that the performance of DP-SGD is governed mainly by the total amount of injected noise, which allows hyperparameters to be tuned at small batch sizes, Panda et al. (2024) propose a linear scaling rule to transfer hyperparameters across privacy budgets, McKenna et al. (2025) derive scaling laws for private language models, and Papernot and Steinke (2022) account for the privacy cost of tuning. Under privacy, the noise dominates Adam’s second-moment estimate, so that DP-Adam behaves like DP-SGD unless corrected ( Tang et al., 2024 ) , and Monzio Compagnoni et al. (2026) compare DP-SignSGD with DP-SGD through stochastic differential equations. For non-private LMO methods, Shulgin et al. (2026) derive hyperparameter scaling laws by minimizing convergence bounds of the same form as Theorem 1 .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Limitations
sections.text: Muon is compatible with differential privacy because, for a scale-invariant update, the leading effect of per-example clipping is a harmless rescaling; the remaining directional bias is controlled by the centered variance alone, which yields convergence guarantees for private momentum-LMO methods in any norm whose clipping floor matches that of clipped SGD up to the norm-conversion constant ρ 1 \rho_{1} . Empirically, privacy makes the batch size the dominant hyperparameter and reorders optimizers, so DP-Muon is most beneficial in some batch-size regimes rather than uniformly. Our analysis has limitations: it assumes an exact LMO rather than a few Newton–Schulz steps and fixed-size batches, whereas our experiments use Poisson subsampling; it treats the Gaussian noise through worst-case dual-norm bounds, which leads to the admissibility condition in ( 3 ) and excludes the hyperparameter regime of our experiments (entirely in the spectral geometry of DP-Muon, and except for CIFAR-10 at the largest batch size in the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} specialization); and its fixed-threshold bound retains a clipping floor. Our language-modeling experiments are small-scale pretraining from scratch; private fine-tuning of pretrained models ( Li et al., 2022a ; Kim and Fan, 2026 ) is a natural next step.

sections.heading: Discussion.
sections.text: Among guarantees for per-example clipping, ours is, to our knowledge, the only one for momentum-LMO dynamics in a general norm that requires only a centered variance bound. Its fixed-noise rate matches the 𝒪 ( K − 1 / 4 ) \mathcal{O}(K^{-1/4}) rate of clipped SGD on the average gradient norm ( Koloskova et al., 2023 ) , which is optimal under bounded variance even without clipping ( Arjevani et al., 2023 ) , up to the ( log ⁡ K ) 1 / 4 (\log K)^{1/4} factor from our high-probability treatment of the privacy noise. Compared with Kim and Fan (2026) , the main differences are as follows. (i) Our clipping floor ρ 1 ​ min ⁡ { σ , σ 2 / c } \rho_{1}\min\{\sigma,\sigma^{2}/c\} vanishes as the sampling noise vanishes, even when ‖ ∇ f ‖ 2 ≫ c \|\nabla f\|_{2}\gg c , because the deterministic part of the clipping bias is a rescaling that the LMO ignores; their residual 𝔼 ​ ( ‖ ∇ f i ‖ − c ) + \mathbb{E}(\|\nabla f_{i}\|-c)_{+} does not vanish in this case. (ii) We need no moment bounds on the raw gradients, which by ( 36 ) would also bound the mean gradient, and no clipping threshold growing with K K . (iii) Our bound holds for any norm and with high probability over the privacy noise. On the other hand, their vanishing rates have no floor (at the price of a growing threshold), and they analyze finite-step Newton–Schulz and a bias-corrected variant, whereas we assume an exact LMO; their rates and ours are therefore not directly comparable. Shanmugam et al. (2026) give a Wedin-type condition under which orthogonalization recovers the leading singular directions of a privatized gradient and document the resulting phase transition empirically; their results concern spectral recovery at a single step rather than convergence of the algorithm.

sections.heading: Muon and LMO-based optimization.
sections.text: Muon applies an approximate polar-factor transformation to a momentum matrix and can be interpreted as stochastic spectral descent ( Carlson et al., 2015 ; Kovalev et al., 2018 ) ; practical implementations use a few Newton–Schulz iterations ( Bernstein, 2025 ; Shulgin et al., 2025 ) , whose effect on convergence is analyzed by Kim and Oh (2026) . The LMO formulation of Pethick et al. (2025) places Muon within a broader class of norm-constrained non-Euclidean methods that includes normalized, sign-based, and coordinate-type updates, extended layer-wise by Gluon ( Riabinin et al., 2025 ) ; trust-region analyses ( Kovalev, 2025 ; Kovalev and Borodich, 2025 ) study the interplay between momentum and noise. For normalized SGD, Cutkosky and Mehta (2020) established the K − 1 / 4 K^{-1/4} rate with momentum, and Cutkosky and Mehta (2021) combined clipping, momentum, and normalization in general normed spaces under heavy-tailed noise, with an additive clipping bias controlled by a growing threshold. Practical and distributed variants include BP-Muon and Drop-Muon ( Khaled et al., 2025 ; Gruntkowska et al., 2025b ) and the distributed or compressed methods Dion, MuLoCo, EF21-Muon, and Compressed Gluon ( Ahn et al., 2025 ; Thérien et al., 2025 ; Gruntkowska et al., 2025a ; Qian et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Clipping, normalization, and private optimization.
sections.text: Clipping and normalization are used to stabilize training ( Pascanu et al., 2013 ; Merity et al., 2017 ; Brown et al., 2020 ; Brock et al., 2021 ) and to limit the influence of unreliable updates in robust distributed optimization ( Karimireddy et al., 2021 ; Malinovsky et al., 2024 ; Islamov et al., 2026 ) . In differential privacy, clipping bounds the sensitivity of each example ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) , also in federated settings ( Geyer et al., 2017 ; McMahan et al., 2018 ; Triastcyn and Faltings, 2019 ) , and makes the gradient estimator biased whenever it is active ( Chen et al., 2020 ; Koloskova et al., 2023 ) . Per-sample normalization ( Bu et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2022 ) removes the dependence on the threshold, and Tang et al. (2024) show that the nonlinear post-processing of noisy gradients by Adam introduces a bias that can be corrected, the analogue of DP-MuonBC ( Kim and Fan, 2026 ) . Monzio Compagnoni et al. (2026) compare DP-SignSGD, the ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} instance of an LMO method, with DP-SGD through stochastic differential equations and find that adaptive methods are preferable at high privacy. Many convergence analyses of private methods simplify clipping through bounded gradients ( Zhang et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2022b ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Lowy et al., 2023 ; Murata and Suzuki, 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , bounded noise or heterogeneity ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Noble et al., 2022 ) , or inactive clipping ( Noble et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) ; Das et al. (2021) study normalized client updates for convex federated objectives. Outside privacy, clipping is analyzed for nonsmooth or fast-growing convex functions ( Shor, 2012 ; Ermoliev, 1988 ; Alber et al., 1998 ) , under generalized smoothness ( Zhang et al., 2019 ; Gorbunov et al., 2024 ; Vankov et al., 2024 ; Lobanov et al., 2024 ; Hübler et al., 2024 ; Tovmasyan et al., 2025 ) , and under heavy-tailed noise ( Gorbunov et al., 2020 ; Nguyen et al., 2023 ) . For private nonconvex optimization with Lipschitz losses, faster rates are obtained with variance reduction or tree aggregation ( Tran and Cutkosky, 2022 ; Arora et al., 2023 ; Lowy et al., 2024 ) , and private Frank–Wolfe-type methods in ℓ p \ell_{p} geometries are studied by Bassily et al. (2021) .

While orthogonalized update rules, such as the recently introduced Muon optimizer, have shown strong empirical performance and scalability, their behavior under Differential Privacy (DP) is not yet understood. In this paper, we propose DP-Muon, a differentially private variant of the Muon optimizer. By analyzing Muon’s orthogonalized updates through the lens of a Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO), we show that the leading effect of per-example clipping is a positive rescaling of the gradient, to which the LMO is blind, so that only a small directional residual controlled by the centered gradient variance enters the optimization error. This yields an 𝒪 ( K − 1 / 4 ) \mathcal{O}(K^{-1/4}) convergence rate, up to logarithmic factors, to a clipping-dependent neighborhood at a fixed noise scale and, with noise calibrated to a fixed ( ε , δ ) (\varepsilon,\delta) budget, the standard ( d / ( n ​ ε ) ) 1 / 2 (\sqrt{d}/(n\varepsilon))^{1/2} privacy–utility bound of DP-SGD, without assuming bounded gradients. Furthermore, we investigate the hyperparameter landscape of DP-Muon and document how the optimal learning rate, momentum, and batch size change under privacy. Empirically, on image classification DP-Muon matches or improves on DP-SGD and DP-Adam, whereas on language modeling the best optimizer depends on the batch size, with DP-Muon best at small batches and DP-Adam best near the privacy-optimal batch size. 1 Introduction Adaptive methods such as Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) and AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017 ) remain the default choice for training large models ( Achiam et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . A prominent recent alternative is Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , which applies an approximate orthogonalization to the momentum of matrix-valued parameters. Muon has attracted considerable attention due to its strong empirical performance, efficient GPU implementation, and reduced optimizer-state memory; its scalability has been demonstrated by training the Moonlight 16B Mixture-of-Experts model on 5.7 trillion tokens ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Its update can be interpreted through stochastic spectral descent ( Carlson et al., 2015 ; Kovalev et al., 2018 ) and, more generally, as a step along a linear minimization oracle (LMO) over a norm ball ( Jaggi, 2013 ; Pethick et al., 2025 ) . The LMO view gives a unified treatment of non-Euclidean methods with momentum, recovering normalized SGD ( Levy, 2016 ; Cutkosky and Mehta, 2020 ) , SignSGD and Signum ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ; Sun et al., 2023 ) , Scion ( Pethick et al., 2025 ) , and Muon as special cases. In this work, we study whether, and how, the advantages of momentum orthogonalization carry over to differential privacy (DP). We consider the standard central, example-level setting of DP-SGD ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) : each per-example gradient is clipped to norm c c , Gaussian noise is added to the average, and the result is passed to the optimizer; the momentum and LMO steps are post-processing and do not affect privacy ( Dwork et al., 2014 ) . The optimization problem, however, becomes substantially more delicate. Active clipping introduces a state-dependent bias, privacy noise is injected at every step, momentum aggregates gradients along a changing trajectory, and the noisy momentum is then passed through a nonlinear map. Existing analyses of private nonconvex optimization typically sidestep active clipping: the sharpest rates assume Lipschitz losses, that is, uniformly bounded per-example gradients, so that clipping at a threshold above the bound is inactive ( Bassily et al., 2021 ; Tran and Cutkosky, 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Arora et al., 2023 ; Lowy et al., 2024 ) , and analyses of private distributed methods make similar assumptions (Appendix F ). Generic analyses of biased stochastic gradients ( Ajalloeian and Stich, 2020 ; Demidovich et al., 2023 ) measure the full additive bias and do not exploit the structure of the update. We compare DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon (along with DP-Scion for language modeling) against their non-private counterparts on CIFAR-10 image classification ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) and on language modeling using a 30M-parameter NanoGPT model. To approximate the orthogonalization update, we utilize the Newton-Schulz method Jordan et al. (2024) with 5 iterations. DP training uses Opacus ( Yousefpour et al., 2021 ) with Poisson subsampling (our analysis uses fixed-size batches), clipping threshold c = 1 c=1 following De et al. (2022) , ε = 8 \varepsilon=8 , and δ = 1 / ( 2 ​ n ) \delta=1/(2n) . For each optimizer and batch size B B we grid-search the learning rate and the momentum 1 − α 1-\alpha , with zero weight decay; grids are listed in Appendix G . To make models compatible with per-example clipping, BatchNorm layers are replaced by GroupNorm and biases are disabled in all linear layers. We report the best value over the grid for each B B . The CIFAR-10 curves average three seeds; all language-modeling results and all heatmaps are single runs. For DP-SGD on CIFAR-10 ( B ≥ 256 B\geq 256 ) and for Scion at B = 16,384 B=16{,}384 , the best learning rate lies at the upper end of the grid (Appendix G ), so these baselines may be slightly under-tuned. Note that the hyperparameter search itself is not included in the privacy accounting, as is common in the DP literature ( Papernot and Steinke, 2022 ) . Second, the gaps between optimizers largely disappear: for 128 ≤ B ≤ 1024 128\leq B\leq 1024 the three curves overlap within one standard deviation. DP-Muon attains the lowest mean loss at every batch size except B = 10000 B=10000 , where DP-SGD is marginally better, but the differences exceed one standard deviation only at the extremes B = 64 B=64 and B = 25000 B=25000 , where DP-Muon degrades the least. Note the different batch-size and loss ranges. Language modeling. The model consists of 6 layers, 6 attention heads, an embedding dimension of 384, and a vocabulary of 50,304 tokens. It is trained on sequences of length 1,024 for 600 million tokens from the 10-billion-token subset of FineWeb ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) , equating to roughly 20 tokens per parameter. The training set is a fixed random subset of n ≈ 5.86 ⋅ 10 5 n\approx 5.86\cdot 10^{5} sequences from this pool, processed for one epoch with Poisson sampling rate q = B / n q=B/n and δ = 1 / ( 2 ​ n ) \delta=1/(2n) ; this translates to approximately 18,300 steps for a batch size of B = 32 B=32 , down to 36 steps for a maximum batch size of B = 16,384 B=16{,}384 . We define a single sequence of 1,024 tokens as the privacy unit, so a document that spans several sequences is not protected as a whole. In the non-private baseline, the performance ranking (Muon < < Adam < < SGD) holds across all batch sizes, and Muon’s advantage grows with B B (achieving a final loss of 4.10 versus 4.82 for Adam at B = 1024 B=1024 ). Under differential privacy (right), the optimal batch size shifts from 32–64 up to 1024–4096, and the optimizer ranking becomes dependent on B B . DP-Muon has the lowest loss for B ≤ 256 B\leq 256 , by at most 0.09 0.09 nats in single runs; DP-Adam is optimal for 512 ≤ B ≤ 2048 512\leq B\leq 2048 and attains the lowest overall loss (6.33 at B = 1024 B=1024 , versus 6.51 for DP-Muon at B = 2048 B=2048 ); and DP-Scion, which utilizes sign updates for the embedding and output layers, performs best for B ≥ 4096 B\geq 4096 and exhibits the least degradation at very large batch sizes. At their respective optimal batch sizes, the four optimizers are within 0.25 nats of each other, compared to a gap of 0.9 nats between Muon and SGD without privacy. What changes under privacy. We highlight three findings. (i) Batch size is the dominant hyperparameter on both tasks: at a fixed budget of epochs or tokens, the optimal batch size grows by a factor of 15–300, and the ranking of optimizers depends on it, so conclusions drawn at a single batch size, or transferred from non-private training, can be misleading. In both tasks the root-mean-square size of the privacy noise exceeds the root-mean-square bound c / B c/\sqrt{B} on the sampling noise of clipped gradients by one to two orders of magnitude at every batch size and decays with B B faster than B − 1 / 2 B^{-1/2} , and the observed optima lie where its norm becomes comparable to the clipping radius (Figure 3 , Appendix D.1 ). There, the noise-to-signal ratio is about 4 4 – 27 27 times larger than the admissibility condition of Theorem 1 allows for 1 − α = 0.9 1-\alpha=0.9 , so the theorem does not cover these configurations and does not explain the location of the optima (Appendix D.2 ). The dependence of the ranking on the batch size is consistent with reports of large gains for private Muon at large batches in vision ( Shanmugam et al., 2026 ) . (ii) The learning rate of DP-Muon grows with the batch size : for language modeling, from 0.05 0.05 at B ≤ 512 B\leq 512 to 0.2 0.2 at B ≥ 8192 B\geq 8192 , whereas the optimal learning rate of DP-Adam stays within [ 10 − 3 , 3 ⋅ 10 − 3 ] [10^{-3},3\cdot 10^{-3}] and, without privacy, the optimal learning rate of every method on language modeling is the same at all batch sizes (Appendix G.3 ). (iii) DP-Muon is insensitive to the momentum : for DP language modeling, at the optimal learning rate, its loss varies by about 0.1 0.1 nats or less over momentum values 1 − α ∈ [ 0.8 , 0.95 ] 1-\alpha\in[0.8,0.95] at every batch size, so the selected momentum appears erratic across batch sizes (Appendix G.3 ).
